lines.s20: Altesino’s Brunello is all Sangiovese from vineyards across Montalcino, aged about three years in big Slavonian oak casks: red and black cherry, plum, violet and wild herbs, firm and bright. Its acidity and grip meet the beef and the rich sauce Espagnole of the Chateau Espagnole.
lines.s45: Brunello di Montalcino is Sangiovese alone, from the hill town of Montalcino south of Siena. Altesino, founded in 1970 at Palazzo Altesi, bottled its Montosoli vineyard on its own in 1975, credited as the first single vineyard Brunello. This is the estate Brunello, blended from vineyards across the zone and aged about three years in large Slavonian casks, so fruit leads, not wood. 2020 was warm and dry, yet the wine is fresh: red and black cherry, plum, violet, wild herbs and tobacco over firm, polished tannin. Its acidity cuts the sauce Espagnole of the Chateau Espagnole; we decant it forty-five minutes and pour at 60 to 64°F.

value.a:
Altesino Brunello di Montalcino 2020 is $150, bin 1747, filed under Italy, Red, Tuscany, Brunello & Rosso di Montalcino, and our classic Brunello.

Brunello di Montalcino, broo-NELL-oh dee mon-tahl-CHEE-noh, is red wine from Sangiovese alone, grown around the hill town of Montalcino south of Siena and aged at least two years in oak before release.

Altesino, ahl-teh-ZEE-noh, was founded in 1970 around Palazzo Altesi, a fifteenth century palazzo in the hills northeast of town. In 1975 it bottled its Montosoli vineyard on its own, credited as the first single vineyard Brunello. This bottle is the estate Brunello, blended from vineyards in several corners of the zone, fermented in steel and aged about three years in large Slavonian oak casks, then some months in bottle.

2020 was a warm, dry summer, and the wines came out fresher than the heat suggested. This one tastes of red and black cherry, plum, violet and wild herbs with a little tobacco, with firm, polished tannin and bright acidity.

The other Altesino line: the Montosoli 2017, bin 18552 at $250, the single vineyard bottling.

value.a:
Asked: Is Brunello a grape?

Answer: Brunello is the old local name for Sangiovese in Montalcino; the wine must be all Sangiovese.

Asked: Is the 2020 ready?

Answer: It is young and firm. Forty-five minutes in a decanter opens it; the sommelier decides on the night.

Asked: How is it different from Chianti?

Answer: Both are Sangiovese, but Brunello comes only from Montalcino, south of the Chianti hills, must be all Sangiovese and ages longer before release, so it is deeper and firmer.

lines.s45: Bordeaux Supérieur is where Médoc vines outside a village name go. Cru Monplaisir is two such parcels just outside Margaux: silt below Château d’Issan, whose team makes our Moulin d’Issan glass, and gravel and clay below Château Margaux. The Gonet-Médeville family of Champagne has owned it since 2009, and the wine is about three quarters Merlot with the two Cabernets. 2022 was a drought year of small, thick skinned berries, and this is ripe and supple: plum, red and black berries, cedar and dark spice. Its plush plum and fine tannin meet the beef and béarnaise of the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak.

value.a:
Cru Monplaisir Bordeaux Supérieur 2022 is $75, bin 34512, filed under France, Bordeaux, Red, Other Bordeaux, and our claret under $100. The list prints it as Cru Montplasir; the label reads Cru Monplaisir, mohn-play-ZEER.

Bordeaux Supérieur covers the whole Bordeaux region, with slightly stricter rules than plain Bordeaux. Cru Monplaisir is two parcels just outside the Margaux appellation: one on silt below Château d’Issan, the other on gravel and clay below Château Margaux. The Gonet-Médeville family of Champagne bought it in 2009.

It is about three quarters Merlot, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc. 2022 in Bordeaux was hot and dry, with small, thick skinned berries and a small crop, yet the wines kept more freshness than the heat suggested. This one is ripe and supple: plum, red and black berries, cedar and dark spice, with fine tannin.

It is the bottle step from our Moulin d’Issan glass, the wine of Château d’Issan’s team: one of Monplaisir’s two parcels lies below that château.

Asked: Is it a Margaux?

Answer: No. Its two parcels lie just outside the Margaux appellation, below Château Margaux and Château d’Issan, so it is labeled Bordeaux Supérieur.

Asked: Is it Cabernet or Merlot?

Answer: Mostly Merlot, about three quarters, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc; the exact mix of the 2022 is a question for the sommelier.

Asked: What does Supérieur mean?

Answer: A Bordeaux with slightly stricter rules than plain Bordeaux: riper grapes and a longer wait before release.

value.style: Grenache led Châteauneuf-du-Pape, made and aged in concrete for fruit and freshness
value.profile: About four fifths Grenache with Syrah and Mourvèdre from several terroirs of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, the rolled stones of the old Rhône bed and sandy safres among them, fermented and aged in concrete vats rather than oak: plum, blackcurrant, black cherry and kirsch with garrigue and a roasted coffee note, round and generous, from a warm, balanced year.
value.guest: Chapoutier’s La Bernardine 2023: Grenache led Châteauneuf-du-Pape, plum, black cherry and garrigue, round and generous, for the lamb shank.
value.goesWith: Lamb, spice and braise: the Lamb Shank en Croûte and its spiced lamb jus, the Creole Hanger Steak and its chili crisp, the Eggs Owen and its red wine braised short rib, and the Petite Filet Mignon.
value.serve: Serve 60 to 64°F in a large red glass, a few minutes in the ice bucket if the room runs warm. Decant about thirty minutes ahead.
value.say: Chapoutier: shah-poo-TYAY; La Bernardine: lah bair-nar-DEEN; Châteauneuf-du-Pape: shah-toh-NUF dew PAHP.
value.why: Our Châteauneuf-du-Pape step from the Durban glass: Grenache led, plum, black cherry and garrigue from a Rhône house guests know, for the Lamb Shank en Croûte and the Creole Hanger Steak.
value.origin: M. Chapoutier is a Tain-l’Hermitage house in the northern Rhône whose history goes back to 1808; La Bernardine, its Châteauneuf-du-Pape, is named for a house among the vines there that the family bought.

lines.s10: Chapoutier’s La Bernardine 2023: Grenache led Châteauneuf-du-Pape, plum, black cherry and garrigue, the bottle step from our Durban glass.
lines.s20: If you are enjoying the Durban, La Bernardine is the step up: Chapoutier’s Châteauneuf-du-Pape, mostly Grenache with Syrah and Mourvèdre, kept in concrete so the fruit stays fresh: plum, black cherry, blackcurrant and garrigue. Round and warm, it loves the spiced lamb jus of the Lamb Shank en Croûte.
lines.s45: Châteauneuf-du-Pape is the Southern Rhône village named for the popes’ summer castle near Avignon. Chapoutier, a Tain-l’Hermitage house whose history goes back to 1808, names La Bernardine for a house among its vines there. About four fifths Grenache with Syrah and Mourvèdre from several terroirs, it is fermented and aged in concrete, not oak, so it tastes of fruit: plum, black cherry, blackcurrant, garrigue and a roasted coffee note. 2023 was warm without the extreme heat of 2022. Our Durban glass is Grenache too; this is its bottle step, generous for the Lamb Shank en Croûte and soft enough for the chili crisp of the Creole Hanger Steak.
lines.sale: La Bernardine is Chapoutier’s Châteauneuf-du-Pape, mostly Grenache with Syrah and Mourvèdre, kept in concrete: plum, black cherry and garrigue, round and warm. For the guest enjoying our Durban glass it is the bottle step, decanted with the Lamb Shank en Croûte and its spiced jus.

value.a:
M. Chapoutier La Bernardine Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2023 is $150, bin 24231, filed under France, Rhône, Red, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, and the bottle step from our Durban glass. The list prints La Bernadine; the label reads La Bernardine, lah bair-nar-DEEN.

Châteauneuf-du-Pape, shah-toh-NUF dew PAHP, is the Southern Rhône village named for the popes’ summer castle near Avignon, where many vineyards lie under large rolled stones that hold the day’s heat.

Chapoutier, shah-poo-TYAY, is a house at Tain-l’Hermitage in the northern Rhône whose history goes back to 1808. It farms its own vines biodynamically and has printed Braille on every label since 1996. La Bernardine is named for a house among the Châteauneuf vines that the family bought. The red is about four fifths Grenache with Syrah and Mourvèdre, from several terroirs of the appellation, fermented and aged in concrete vats rather than oak.

2023 was warm without the extreme heat of 2022. This one tastes of plum, black cherry, blackcurrant and garrigue, with a roasted coffee note, round and generous.

Our house sheet says a guest who likes Châteauneuf-du-Pape will enjoy the Durban by the glass; La Bernardine is that Châteauneuf, by the bottle.

value.a:
Asked: Is it like the Durban?

Answer: Both are Grenache led reds of the Southern Rhône. La Bernardine is Châteauneuf-du-Pape: fuller, warmer and longer.

Asked: Why is there Braille on the label?

Answer: Chapoutier has printed Braille on its labels since 1996, honoring a family link with Maurice de la Sizeranne, who devised an abridged form of Braille.

Asked: Is it oaky?

Answer: No. By the house’s recent sheets it is made and aged in concrete vats, so it tastes of fruit and spice, not wood.

value.a: The list prints La Bernadine; the label reads La Bernardine. Bin 24231 is also printed for the Luigi Tecce Puro Sangue Riserva Taurasi 2018, so ring it in by bin and pull by name and vintage. Chapoutier also makes a white La Bernardine, not on our list: check that the bottle is the red. Les Meysonniers 2024, printed Les Maysonniers at bin 23742, is Chapoutier’s Crozes-Hermitage Syrah, not this wine. One trade source says La Bernardine sees oak; the sheets for recent vintages say concrete, so leave the question to the sommelier. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

value.a: Present the bottle and say M. Chapoutier, La Bernardine, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, 2023, shah-poo-TYAY. Decant it about thirty minutes ahead and serve at 60 to 64°F in large red glasses, a few minutes in the ice bucket if the room runs warm, since warm Grenache shows its alcohol. Pour a taste for the host, then the guests, the host last. Say: “La Bernardine 2023: Châteauneuf-du-Pape, plum, black cherry and garrigue.”
